fields.definition: An audible click or transient artifact produced when an envelope generator changes a signal's level too abruptly, creating a step discontinuity in the waveform. It typically occurs with a near-instantaneous attack or release, or when a note is gated on or off at a non-zero point in the cycle.
fields.plain_english: An envelope click is a short popping sound. It happens when a note's volume jumps up or down too fast for the speaker to follow it smoothly, leaving a tiny step in the wave that you hear as a click.
fields.purpose_function: The term names a discontinuity created by envelope shaping so technicians can recognise it; a click signals that an attack or release stage is too fast for the signal to settle, which is fixed by adding a short fade ramp.
fields.practical_application: When a synth or sampler clicks on every note, a technician lengthens the attack or release by a few milliseconds, or enables the instrument's click-reduction or zero-crossing option, to smooth the transition.
common_mistakes: Setting attack and release to zero and assuming the sound stays clean, when instant level jumps cause clicks
Blaming the oscillator, a cable, or a fault for a click that actually comes from envelope timing
Confusing an intentional percussive transient with an unwanted envelope click
scenario_contexts: A bass patch with instant attack clicks on every note during a live set
Gating a pad on and off in a DAW produces pops at each edit point
A sampler clicks when its loop points or note-offs land at non-zero waveform values

sources: Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Sound on Sound, Synth Secrets (Gordon Reid)

fields.definition: Filter resonance is a boost in level applied to frequencies near a filter's cutoff frequency, created by feedback within the filter. Raising resonance (often labelled Q) narrows and emphasises that band, and at high settings the filter can self-oscillate into a sine-like tone.
fields.plain_english: Resonance makes the frequencies right around the filter's cutoff point louder, adding a sharp, ringing peak. Turn it up too far and the filter starts to whistle a tone all by itself.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a designer emphasise a chosen frequency band and add character or bite to a filter, especially during a sweep; it exists because feedback around the cutoff shapes the timbre far more than a plain filter slope alone.
fields.practical_application: A synth player raises resonance while sweeping the cutoff to create classic squelchy, vocal, or wah-like movement in a lead or bass, while watching for harsh peaks or self-oscillation that could overload a channel.
common_mistakes: Confusing the resonance (Q) control with the cutoff frequency control
UNSAFE: pushing resonance into self-oscillation at high output can produce a loud sustained tone that risks hearing damage and driver stress
Assuming more resonance always sounds better, when it can create harsh, thin, or unstable peaks
Not allowing for the level boost resonance adds near cutoff, causing clipping
scenario_contexts: Dialing a squelchy acid bassline by combining high resonance with a moving cutoff
Using a resonant peak to make a filter sweep more dramatic in a build-up
A resonant filter self-oscillating and used as a tunable sine source

sources: Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)

fields.definition: Frequency modulation (FM) is the varying of a carrier signal's instantaneous frequency in proportion to a modulating signal. In synthesis, when the modulator runs at audio rate it generates sidebands spaced around the carrier, producing rich, often inharmonic tones from a small number of oscillators (operators).
fields.plain_english: In FM, one wave keeps speeding up and slowing down another wave very fast. This adds many new tones, so you can build bright, bell-like, or metallic sounds from just a few simple waves.
fields.purpose_function: FM exists to generate complex, evolving spectra efficiently; a few operators can produce sounds such as bells, electric pianos, and gritty basses that would need many oscillators with other methods.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer programs FM by choosing operator frequency ratios and modulation depth (index) to shape the harmonics, as on Yamaha DX-series hardware or modern FM plug-ins, to build electric pianos, bells, and aggressive basses.
common_mistakes: Confusing audio-rate FM synthesis with slow LFO vibrato, which is also frequency modulation but stays sub-audio
Assuming operator ratios do not matter, when they set whether the result is harmonic or clangorous
Expecting FM to behave like subtractive synthesis and reaching for a filter instead of adjusting the modulation index
scenario_contexts: Programming a DX7-style electric piano by tuning operator ratios and envelopes
Adding a modulator at audio rate to an oscillator to create metallic bell tones
Using cross-modulation between two oscillators to make aggressive bass timbres

sources: Chowning, The Synthesis of Complex Audio Spectra by Means of Frequency Modulation, JAES 21(7), 1973 (AES)
Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)

fields.definition: LFO wobble is the pulsing, undulating change in timbre or level produced when a low-frequency oscillator (LFO) modulates a parameter, most often filter cutoff, at a sub-audio rate. Syncing the LFO to tempo produces the rhythmic 'wobble bass' associated with dubstep and related styles.
fields.plain_english: A wobble is that pulsing, throbbing sound you hear when a slow control wave opens and closes a filter over and over. Matching its speed to the beat gives you the classic dubstep wobble bass.
fields.purpose_function: It turns a static tone into rhythmic, moving texture; the LFO automates repeated parameter changes so the sound pulses in time without the player moving a control by hand.
fields.practical_application: A producer routes a tempo-synced LFO to a low-pass filter's cutoff and adjusts the rate and depth to make a bass patch wobble in time with the track, often switching LFO rates from section to section.
common_mistakes: Leaving the LFO free-running so the wobble drifts out of time with the beat
Setting LFO depth so high the filter fully closes and the sound drops out
Confusing LFO wobble (sub-audio modulation) with FM, where the modulator runs at audio rate
scenario_contexts: Building a dubstep wobble bass with a tempo-synced LFO on filter cutoff
Adding slow LFO movement to a pad so it breathes over time
Assigning different LFO rates to a mod wheel to perform wobble changes live

sources: Sound on Sound, Synth Secrets (Gordon Reid)
Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)

fields.definition: A modulation sweep is a continuous, gradual change of a parameter over time driven by a modulation source such as an envelope, LFO, or manual control. The most common example is a filter sweep, where cutoff frequency moves smoothly across the spectrum.
fields.plain_english: A modulation sweep is a smooth, gliding change to a control, like slowly opening a filter from dark to bright. It is the rising or falling movement you hear in build-ups and transitions.
fields.purpose_function: It adds motion and tension by changing a setting gradually rather than in one step; sweeps are a core way to create build-ups, transitions, and evolving textures.
fields.practical_application: An engineer automates a control, or uses an envelope or LFO, to sweep filter cutoff or another parameter upward through a build, then resets it at the drop, to shape energy across a song section.
common_mistakes: Sweeping too fast, so the movement sounds like a click or jump instead of a smooth glide
Forgetting that resonance greatly changes how a filter sweep sounds
Confusing a one-time envelope sweep with a repeating LFO cycle
scenario_contexts: Automating a filter cutoff sweep to build tension before a drop
Using an envelope to sweep pitch or cutoff at the start of each note
Sweeping a phaser or wah parameter across a guitar solo

sources: Sound on Sound, Synth Secrets (Gordon Reid)
Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
